messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Emil had always been a private person, but after the physical abuse he suffered at the hands of his caregiver during childhood, he became increasingly withdrawn. The memories of those events still lingered, and certain triggers would send him spiraling back to that vulnerable state. A specific temperature on his skin, for instance, would transport him to the cold, damp cellar where he was often locked away. His heart racing or pounding would also bring back the panic he felt during those episodes of abuse. But it was the sudden, intrusive memories of the event that left him reeling – images of his caregiver's face, twisted in anger, would flash before his eyes without warning. As these triggers intensified, Emil began to feel a growing sense of threat. He started noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment – a hammer on the workbench, a sharp edge on the kitchen counter. His body would react before he even had time to think, leaving him with a constant feeling of being "on edge." Even an unexpected touch from his wife, Maria, could startle him, making him flinch away in alarm. Emil couldn't shake the feeling that he was constantly walking on eggshells, waiting for the next blow. He became convinced that people couldn't be trusted – not even those closest to him. "You never know what can happen next," he would tell himself, a mantra of constant vigilance that left him exhausted. This sense of being an outsider, looking in at a world that seemed hostile and unforgiving, only added to his anxiety. As Emil struggled to cope with these feelings, he began to develop maladaptive strategies to avoid the triggers and threats that seemed omnipresent. He stopped paying attention to or looking at his own body, fearing what memories it might stir up. Social contacts became increasingly difficult – seeing people he had socialized with before the event only served as a painful reminder of what he had lost. And physical contact? That was out of the question altogether. But these strategies only seemed to reinforce Emil's negative appraisals. He felt like an outsider, stuck on the periphery of life, unable to connect with others or even himself. The more he avoided his own body and social contacts, the more convinced he became that people couldn't be trusted – that they were all just waiting for him to let his guard down so they could pounce. As this cycle intensified, Emil found himself back in the grip of those triggers that had started it all – memories of the event, a racing heart, a sudden chill on his skin. The threat he felt was palpable, and his body reacted before he even had time to think. It was as if he was trapped in a never-ending loop, with no escape from the pain and fear that haunted him. It was this desperation that finally brought Emil to seek help – the realization that he couldn't keep living like this, constantly on edge, waiting for the next blow. As he sat in his therapist's office, he looked around nervously, noticing the potential dangers lurking in every corner. But he knew he had to try to break free from this cycle of fear and mistrust. He was tired of being an outsider, looking in at a world that seemed hostile and unforgiving. It was time for Emil to take back control, to learn to trust himself – and maybe, just maybe, others – once again.
